question.text: Under which of the following circumstances can an open offer, once made, be withdrawn?

answer.text: When the target company's stock price drops by more than 25%
When the acquirer finds adverse information during due diligence
When a statutory approval required for the acquisition is refused
When the acquirer receives a better acquisition opportunity elsewhere

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook permits withdrawal of an open offer only in narrow circumstances: (i) statutory approvals required for the acquisition and disclosed in the Detailed Public Statement / Letter of Offer are finally refused; (ii) the acquirer, being a natural person, dies; (iii) a condition stipulated in the underlying agreement attracting the obligation to make an open offer is not met for reasons outside the reasonable control of the acquirer and the agreement is rescinded; or (iv) SEBI, by a reasoned order, permits withdrawal in such other circumstances as it deems fit. The Trap: A stock-price decline or adverse due-diligence findings are not listed grounds for withdrawal — the regime is deliberately restrictive so that shareholders who have acted in reliance on the public announcement are protected. Note: Refusal of a statutory approval must be final (not interim) and must relate to an approval that was disclosed in the DPS or Letter of Offer.
